analysis.one_liner: Restores federal pre-approval for election rule changes in states with recent voting-rights violations.
analysis.headline: Introduced July 29, 2025 and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where no vote has been scheduled; all 47 supporting senators are Democrats or independents [S1][S4][S5].
analysis.plain_summary: The bill revives the part of the Voting Rights Act that required certain states and localities to get federal approval before changing election rules — a system the Supreme Court shelved in 2013 when it struck down the old coverage formula. Under this bill, any state with 15 voting-rights violations in the last 25 years (or 10, including one by the state itself) would need approval from the Justice Department or a federal court before putting major voting changes into effect, for a 10-year period [S2]. It also tightens the legal standards for proving vote discrimination, requires public notice of election changes, lets the Justice Department demand election documents during investigations, and adds criminal penalties for intimidating election workers [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Voters — particularly voters of color and language-minority voters — in states and localities with recent records of voting-rights violations. They gain a federal checkpoint before restrictive rules like new ID requirements, polling place closures, or redistricting plans take effect, plus clearer court standards for challenging discriminatory rules [S2][S3]. Election workers also gain new protection against threats and intimidation [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters in jurisdictions with discrimination records

how_it_helps.text: States and political subdivisions must obtain preclearance from the Justice Department or a federal court before implementing covered voting changes, with coverage triggered by 15 voting-rights violations in 25 years, or 10 including one by the state itself; subdivisions with 3 or more violations are covered separately [S2].

The bill strengthens the standards courts use in vote-dilution and vote-denial cases, restores the 'totality of circumstances' factors, and lets courts block practices that were enacted with a discriminatory purpose even partly [S3].
States and localities must publicly disclose changes to voting rules, polling place resources, and district boundaries, in formats accessible to voters with disabilities [S3].
The bill adds new criminal penalties — fines up to $2,500 and up to 6 months in jail — for anyone who uses force or threats to intimidate voters, poll watchers, or election officials [S3].

analysis.who_pays: State and local election officials in covered jurisdictions, who must submit major voting changes for pre-approval, publish detailed public notices, and respond to Justice Department document demands. States and legislatures covered by the formula lose the ability to change election rules and district maps without federal sign-off [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Covered states and localities would face significant administrative burdens: preclearance reviews, 48-hour public-notice requirements, and Justice Department demands for election documents, which critics see as federal control over election administration that has traditionally been run by the states [S3].

The formula covers jurisdictions based on their violation records over 25 years, which critics argue is an open-ended expansion of federal oversight; the bill's grants to small jurisdictions (population 10,000 or less) partially offset compliance costs for the smallest localities [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a working federal checkpoint against voting rules that discriminate, aimed at jurisdictions with documented recent violations rather than a fixed list. The costs are real but administrative: extra paperwork, pre-approval delays, and federal oversight of decisions states have made on their own since 2013. The strongest objection is that the formula subjects states to federal supervision based on past conduct, which critics call unfair to states that have changed; supporters counter that the formula expires for jurisdictions that stay violation-free and can be exited through court approval.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on July 29, 2025, and has stayed there — no committee vote, no floor debate [S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Dick Durbin introduced the John R. Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act of 2025 on July 29, 2025, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary [S5].
As of the latest action record, no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — has been taken since the committee referral [S5].
The bill has 46 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents, with no Republican support in the Senate [S4].

The bill responds to the Supreme Court's 2013 Shelby County v. Holder decision, which struck down the old formula for deciding which states needed preclearance, leaving that part of the Voting Rights Act unenforceable until Congress writes a new formula.
Previous versions of this bill passed the House in 2021 but failed to break a Senate filibuster, falling short of the 60 votes needed to proceed, 50-48.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Jurisdictions and officeholders who benefit from the current rules — no preclearance, no new federal review of election changes — are better off so far, since the bill has not moved and its lack of Republican support gives it no clear path in a Senate that usually needs 60 votes to advance legislation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Current officeholders, no new voting oversight

for.name: Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 29, 2025 and shepherded it to the Judiciary Committee, which he chairs.

for.name: 46 Senate Democrats and independents
for.role: Original cosponsors, including Sen. Chuck Schumer and Sen. Raphael Warnock
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill support from every Democrat and independent in the Senate caucus at introduction [S4].

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Has not supported the bill; no Republican senator has cosponsored it, and Senate Republicans' earlier refusal to advance similar voting rights legislation left the John Lewis Act short of the 60 votes needed to proceed in 2021.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 47 sponsors and cosponsors is a Democrat or independent; no Republican has signed on [S4].

industries.industry: State legislatures and state/local election officials
industries.note: Covered jurisdictions would need federal pre-approval before changing election rules and would face new notice and document-production requirements. Their interest in maximum discretion over election rules runs against the bill's goal of checking discriminatory changes before they take effect.

industries.industry: Political parties and mapmakers who redraw district lines
industries.note: In covered jurisdictions, redistricting plans and boundary changes that shift minority voting strength would require preclearance, limiting how maps can be redrawn. Each discriminatory district or plan would count as an independent violation under the coverage formula.
Jurisdictions with populations of 10,000 or less are eligible for federal grants to help pay for the bill's public-notice compliance requirements.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors and the Senate usually requiring 60 votes to end debate on most bills, the realistic path is that the bill stays in the Judiciary Committee without a markup or floor vote for the rest of this Congress, as similar bills did in prior sessions. It could move only if bipartisan support develops.
